Gary's Take

Afternoon baseball at Busch Stadium, with the Giants and Cardinals settling a split series. St. Louis gets the favorite’s billing, but I’m taking San Francisco at +136 because the starting matchup gives this underdog a credible route to taking control. The Cardinals’ starter carries a 5.53 ERA and 1.49 WHIP, with 27 home runs allowed in 143.1 IP. Those are season results, not a prediction of another rough outing. But they describe substantial vulnerability over a meaningful sample, and I don’t see enough protection elsewhere in this matchup to justify backing St. Louis at -162.

The Giants’ second hitter supplies a specific reason to trust their offensive opportunity: an .880 OPS against left-handed pitching in 118 AB. The opposing starter has allowed an .832 OPS to left-handed hitters, so this matchup offers more encouragement than an automatic assumption that a lefty neutralizes a left-handed bat. That is supporting evidence for this particular lineup, without pretending one hitter settles the game. The hot afternoon and wind blowing toward center add another consideration for a starter whose home-run allowance is already substantial. Those conditions help both offenses, but they reinforce the importance of that vulnerability.

The strongest argument against San Francisco is the Cardinals’ middle-of-the-order production against right-handed pitching, backed by principal late-inning relievers who sat out yesterday. The Giants’ starter also has a 5.24 ERA in just 22.1 IP; his lower WHIP does not establish a dependable pitching advantage. That keeps my confidence modest. Still, San Francisco’s principal closing option also sat out yesterday, leaving a plausible relief path if the offense establishes a lead. My call is that the Giants generate enough damage against the starting pitching to put that path into play. At +136, I’m backing that outcome despite St. Louis’ credible offensive counterargument.

Gary's Take

The series finale is set at Rogers Centre, with Detroit chasing the sweep and Toronto looking to answer back. I’m taking Detroit at +112, and the strongest reason is how its confirmed lineup matches Scherzer’s results against left-handed hitters. He has allowed an .848 OPS to lefties compared with .624 to righties. Kevin McGonigle, Colt Keith and Riley Greene give Detroit left-handed bats throughout the upper part of the order, with Max Clark and Brett Callahan adding more. That matchup gives me a concrete reason to back the underdog beyond simply comparing the starters’ ERAs.

Montero’s 1.03 WHIP against Scherzer’s 1.37 strengthens that read: Detroit’s starter has allowed fewer baserunners, and Toronto’s right-handed hitters face his stronger season split. Montero has allowed a .570 OPS to righties versus .672 to lefties. Detroit’s recent offensive results also have some support in the quality of its contact. Over the last three games, its hard-hit rate was 39.0%, compared with Toronto’s 25.6%. That is a small sample, so it supports the current form without establishing a new offensive baseline. The series has included a close Detroit win and a blowout; today’s pitching and lineup matchup carry more weight for me than the opportunity to finish a sweep.

The strongest argument against Detroit is Toronto keeping the game close behind Scherzer and then turning to Louis Varland and Tyler Rogers. Neither pitched yesterday, so the Blue Jays have a plausible late-inning answer despite the work demanded of other relievers. Detroit also has to account for Kyle Finnegan’s consecutive appearances. But Tyler Holton and Kenley Jansen were unused yesterday, giving the Tigers their own potential route through the closing innings. I respect Toronto’s bullpen counterargument. At +112, though, Detroit’s lineup fit and Montero’s lower baserunner allowance outweigh it for me.
